modern:
Downcast and troubled Christian, come and glean today in the broad field of promise. Here are plenty of precious promises that exactly meet your needs. Take this one: “He will not break the bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax.” Doesn’t that suit your case? A reed, helpless, insignificant and weak; a bruised reed, that no music can come out of; weaker than weakness itself; a reed, and that reed bruised; yet he won’t break you. On the contrary, he will restore and strengthen you. You are like the smoking flax: no light, no warmth can come from you; but he won’t quench you. He will blow with his sweet breath of mercy until he fans you into a flame.

Would you like to glean another ear? “Come unto me all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” What soft words! Your heart is tender, and the Master knows it, and so he speaks to you so gently. Won’t you obey him and come to him, even now? Take another ear of grain: “Fear not, thou worm Jacob, I will help thee, saith the Lord and thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.” How can you be afraid with such a wonderful assurance as this? You can gather ten thousand golden ears like these! “I have blotted out thy sins like a cloud, and like a thick cloud thy transgressions.” Or this: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.” Or this: “The Spirit and the Bride say, Come, and let him that is athirst come, and whosoever will let him take the water of life freely.” Our Master’s field is very rich; look at the handfuls! See, there they lie in front of you, poor timid believer! Gather them up, make them your own, for Jesus tells you to take them. Don’t be afraid; only believe! Grasp these sweet promises, thresh them out by meditation, and feed on them with joy.

notes.note: To glean was to gather the stalks of grain the reapers left behind, the right of the poor under Israel’s law ([[Ruth.2.2|Ruth 2:2]]). Corn means grain.

modern:
All year round, every hour of every day, God is richly blessing us; whether we sleep or wake, his mercy attends us. The sun may leave us a legacy of darkness, but our God never stops shining on his children with beams of love. Like a river, his loving kindness is always flowing, with a fullness as inexhaustible as his own nature. Like the air that always surrounds the earth, always ready to support human life, the kindness of God surrounds all his creatures; in it, as in their element, they live and move and have their being. Yet just as the sun on summer days cheers us with warmer and brighter beams than at other times, and rivers swell with rain at certain seasons, and the air itself is sometimes charged with fresher, more bracing or more balmy influences than before, so it is with the mercy of God. It has its golden hours, its days of overflowing, when the Lord shows the greatness of his grace before the sons of men.

Among the blessings of the lower springs, *the joyful days of harvest* are a special season of overflowing favor. It is the glory of autumn that the ripe gifts of providence are given in abundance then; it is the mellow season when hopes come true, whereas everything before was only hope and expectation. Great is the joy of harvest. Happy are the reapers who fill their arms with heaven’s generosity. The psalmist tells us that the harvest is the crowning of the year. Surely these crowning mercies call for crowning thanksgiving! Let’s give it in *the inward feelings of gratitude*. Let our hearts be warmed; let our spirits remember, meditate and think about this goodness of the Lord. Then let’s *praise him with our lips*, and praise and magnify the name of the one from whose bounty all this goodness flows. Let’s glorify God by giving *our gifts* to his cause. A practical proof of our gratitude is a special thank-offering to the Lord of the harvest.

modern:
Our belief in God’s wisdom assumes, and requires, that he has a settled purpose and plan in the work of salvation. What would *creation* have been without his design? Is there a fish in the sea or a bird in the air that was left to chance in its making? No; in every bone, joint and muscle, sinew, gland and blood vessel, you see the presence of a God working everything according to the design of infinite wisdom. And will God be present in creation, ruling over all, and not in *grace*? Will the new creation have the fickle genius of free will presiding over it, when divine counsel rules the old creation?

Look at *providence*! Who doesn’t know that not a sparrow falls to the ground without your Father? Even the hairs of your head are all numbered. God weighs the mountains of our grief in scales, and the hills of our trouble in balances. And will there be a God in providence and not in grace? Will the shell be planned by wisdom and the kernel be left to blind chance? No; he knows the end from the beginning. He sees in its appointed place not only the cornerstone he has laid in fair colors, in the blood of his dear Son, but each of the chosen stones taken out of the quarry of nature and polished by his grace, in its ordained position. He sees the whole from corner to cornice, from base to roof, from foundation to pinnacle. He has in his mind a clear knowledge of every stone that will be laid in its prepared space, how vast the building will be, and when the topstone will be brought out with shouts of “Grace! Grace! unto it.” At the last it will be clearly seen that in every chosen vessel of mercy Jehovah did as he willed with his own, and that in every part of the work of grace he accomplished his purpose and glorified his own name.

modern:
Let me learn from Ruth the gleaner. As she went out to gather the ears of grain, so I must go out into the fields of prayer, meditation, the ordinances and hearing the word, to gather spiritual food. *The gleaner gathers her share ear by ear*; her gains come little by little. So I must be content to search for single truths, if there is no greater plenty of them. Every ear helps make a bundle, and every gospel lesson helps make us wise to salvation. *The gleaner keeps her eyes open*: if she stumbled about the stubble in a dream, she would have no load to carry home happily in the evening. I must be watchful in my religious exercises, or they will do me no good. I fear I have lost a great deal already. Oh, that I may value my opportunities rightly and glean more diligently!

*The gleaner stoops for everything she finds*, and so must I. Lofty spirits criticize and object, but lowly minds glean and benefit. A humble heart is a great help toward hearing the gospel with profit. The implanted word that saves the soul can only be received with meekness. A stiff back makes a bad gleaner. Down, Master Pride! You are a vile robber, not to be put up with for a moment. *What the gleaner gathers, she holds*: if she dropped one ear to find another, her day’s work would come to very little. She is as careful to keep as to get, and so in the end her gains are great. How often I forget everything I hear! The second truth pushes the first out of my head, and so my reading and hearing end in much ado about nothing. Do I really feel how important it is to store up the truth? A hungry stomach makes the gleaner wise: if there is no grain in her hand, there will be no bread on her table. She works with a sense of necessity, and so her step is quick and her grip is firm. I have an even greater necessity. Lord, help me feel it, so that it may urge me on to glean in fields that give so rich a reward to diligence.

modern:
Quietly think about the Lamb as the light of heaven. In Scripture, light is the picture of *joy*. The joy of the saints in heaven is summed up in this: *Jesus* chose us, loved us, bought us, cleansed us, clothed us, kept us, glorified us; we are there entirely through the Lord Jesus. Each of these thoughts will be to them like a cluster of the grapes of Eshcol. Light is also the cause of *beauty*. Nothing of beauty is left when the light has gone. Without light no radiance flashes from the sapphire, no gentle gleam comes from the pearl; and so all the beauty of the saints above comes from Jesus. Like planets, they reflect the light of the Sun of Righteousness; they live as beams coming from the central sun. If he withdrew, they would die; if his glory were veiled, their glory would go out.

Light is also the picture of *knowledge*. In heaven our knowledge will be perfect, but the Lord Jesus himself will be its fountain. Dark providences, never understood before, will be clearly seen then, and everything that puzzles us now will become plain to us in the light of the Lamb. Oh, what revelations there will be, and what glorifying of the God of love! Light also means *manifestation*: light shows things up. In this world it doesn’t yet appear what we will be. God’s people are a hidden people; but when Christ receives his people into heaven, he will touch them with the wand of his own love and change them into the image of his revealed glory. They were poor and wretched, but what a transformation! They were stained with sin, but one touch of his finger, and they are as bright as the sun and as clear as crystal. Oh, what a manifestation! All this comes from the exalted Lamb. Whatever radiant splendor there may be, Jesus will be the center and soul of it all. Oh, to be there and see him in his own light, the King of kings and Lord of lords!

modern:
Jesus is making his way through the crowd to the house of Jairus, to raise the synagogue ruler’s dead daughter; but he is so lavish in goodness that he works another miracle on the way. While this rod of Aaron is still in bud with a wonder not yet done, it bears the ripe almonds of a finished work of mercy. For us, it is enough to have one purpose and go straight off and carry it out; it would be unwise to spend our energies along the way. Hurrying to rescue a drowning friend, we can’t afford to exhaust our strength on someone else in the same danger. It is enough for a tree to bear one kind of fruit, and for a man to fulfill his own particular calling. But our Master knows no limit of power and no boundary to his mission. He is so overflowing with grace that, like the sun, which shines as it rolls on in its orbit, his path is radiant with loving kindness. He is a swift arrow of love, which not only reaches its appointed target but perfumes the air it flies through. Power is always going out of Jesus, as sweet scents breathe out from flowers, and it always will be flowing from him, like water from a sparkling fountain.

What delightful encouragement this truth gives us! If our Lord is so ready to heal the sick and bless the needy, then, my soul, don’t be slow to put yourself in his way, so that he may smile on you. Don’t be slack in asking, if he is so generous in giving. Pay close attention to his word, now and always, so that Jesus may speak through it to your heart. Wherever he is to be found, go there, so that you may get his blessing. When he is present to heal, won’t he heal you? But surely he is present even now, for he always comes to hearts that need him. And don’t you need him? Ah, *he* knows how much! Son of David, turn your eye and look on the distress in front of you now, and make your petitioner whole.

modern:
Every believer understands that to know God is the highest and best kind of knowledge; and this spiritual knowledge is a source of strength to the Christian. It strengthens his *faith*. Scripture constantly speaks of believers as people who are enlightened and taught by the Lord. They are said to “have an unction from the Holy One,” and it is the Spirit’s special work to lead them into all truth, all to increase and nourish their faith. Knowledge strengthens *love* as well as faith. Knowledge opens the door, and through that door we see our Savior. Or, to use another picture, knowledge paints the portrait of Jesus, and when we see that portrait, then we love him. We can’t love a Christ we don’t know, at least to some degree. If we know only a little of the excellent qualities of Jesus, of what he has done for us and what he is doing now, we can’t love him much; but the more we know him, the more we will love him.

Knowledge also strengthens *hope*. How can we hope for something if we don’t know it exists? Hope may be the telescope, but until we are taught, our ignorance stands in front of the lens and we can see nothing at all. Knowledge takes away what is in the way, and when we look through the bright lens we see the glory to be revealed and look forward to it with joyful confidence. Knowledge gives us reasons for *patience*. How can we have patience unless we know something of Christ’s sympathy, and understand the good that is to come out of the correction our heavenly Father sends us? And there isn’t a single Christian grace that, under God, won’t be nourished and brought to perfection by holy knowledge. How important it is, then, that we grow not only in grace but in the “knowledge” of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

modern: How destructive hail is to the standing crops, beating the precious grain out onto the ground! How grateful we should be when the grain is spared so terrible a ruin! Let’s give the Lord thanks. Even more to be dreaded are those mysterious destroyers smut, bunt, rust and mildew. They turn the ear into a mass of soot, or make it rot, or dry up the grain, and all in a way so far beyond human control that the farmer is forced to cry, “This is the finger of God.” Countless tiny fungi do the damage, and if it weren’t for the goodness of God, the rider on the black horse would soon scatter famine over the land. Infinite mercy spares the food of men; but in view of the active agents ready to destroy the harvest, we are very wisely taught to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread.” The curse is abroad; we constantly need the blessing. When blight and mildew come, they are discipline from heaven, and men must learn to hear the rod and the one who has appointed it.

Spiritually, mildew is no rare evil. When our work looks most promising, this blight appears. We hoped for many conversions, and instead, look: general apathy, overflowing worldliness or a cruel hardness of heart! There may be no open sin in those we are working for, but there is a lack of sincerity and decision that sadly disappoints our hopes. We learn from this our dependence on the Lord, and our need to pray that no blight may fall on our work. Spiritual pride or laziness will soon bring this dreadful evil on us, and only the Lord of the harvest can remove it. Mildew may even attack our own hearts and shrivel our prayers and religious exercises. May it please the great Gardener to turn away so serious a disaster. Shine, blessed Sun of Righteousness, and drive the blights away.

modern:
On some points a believer is absolutely sure. He knows, for instance, that God sits in the stern of the boat when it rocks most. He believes that an unseen hand is always on the world’s tiller, and that wherever providence may drift, Jehovah steers it. That reassuring knowledge prepares him for everything. He looks over the raging waters and sees the spirit of Jesus walking on the waves, and he hears a voice saying, “It is I, be not afraid.” He knows too that God is always wise, and knowing this, he is confident that there can be no accidents and no mistakes; that nothing can happen that ought not to. He can say, “If I should lose everything I have, it is better for me to lose than to have, if God so wills. The worst disaster is the wisest and kindest thing that could happen to me, if God ordains it.”

“We know that all things work together for good to them that love God.” The Christian doesn’t merely hold this as a theory; *he knows it* as a fact. Everything *has* worked for good so far. The poisonous drugs, mixed in the right proportions, have brought the cure; the sharp cuts of the surgeon’s knife have cleaned out the proud flesh and helped the healing. Every event so far has worked out the most divinely blessed results; and so, believing that God rules everything, that he governs wisely, that he brings good out of evil, the believer’s heart is assured, and he is enabled to meet each trial calmly as it comes. In the spirit of true surrender the believer can pray, “Send me what you will, my God, as long as it comes from you. No bad portion ever came from your table to any of your children.”

modern:
Family ties bring obligations. The Reubenites and Gadites would have been unbrotherly if they had claimed the land already conquered and left the rest of the people to fight for their shares alone. We have received a great deal through the efforts and sufferings of the saints in years gone by, and if we don’t make some return to the church of Christ by giving her our best energies, we aren’t worthy to be enrolled in her ranks. Others are fighting the errors of the age bravely, or digging out perishing people from the ruins of the fall; and if we fold our hands in idleness, we need to be warned, or the curse of Meroz may fall on us. The Master of the vineyard says, “Why stand ye here all the day idle?” What is the idler’s excuse? Personal service to Jesus becomes all the more everyone’s duty because some give it so cheerfully and abundantly. The labors of devoted missionaries and fervent ministers shame us if we sit still in laziness.

Shrinking from trial is the temptation of those who are at ease in Zion. They would gladly escape the cross and still wear the crown, and the question for this evening’s meditation fits them very well. If the most precious are tested in the fire, are we to escape the crucible? If the diamond must be ground on the wheel, are we to be made perfect without suffering? Who has commanded the wind to stop blowing because our boat is on the sea? Why on earth should we be treated better than our Lord? The firstborn felt the rod, so why not the younger brothers? It is a cowardly pride that would choose a downy pillow and a silk couch for a soldier of the cross. Far wiser is the one who, first resigned to God’s will, grows by the energy of grace to be pleased with it, and so learns to gather lilies at the foot of the cross and, like Samson, to find honey in the lion.

modern: *What enemies are about*? Errors are a numerous horde, and new ones appear every hour: which heresy must I be on guard against? Sins creep out of their hiding places when darkness reigns; I must climb the watchtower myself and watch in prayer. Our heavenly Protector foresees all the attacks that are about to be made on us, and while the evil planned against us is still only in Satan’s desire, he prays for us that our faith won’t fail when we are sifted like wheat. Keep warning us of our enemies, gracious Watchman, and for Zion’s sake don’t keep silent.

“Watchman, what of the night?” *What weather is coming* for the church? Are the clouds gathering, or is it all clear and fair overhead? We must care for the church of God with anxious love; and now that Roman Catholicism and unbelief are both threatening, let’s watch the signs of the times and get ready for conflict.

“Watchman, what of the night?” *What stars can be seen*? What precious promises suit our present case? You sound the alarm; give us the comfort too. Christ, the North Star, is always fixed in his place, and all the stars are secure in the right hand of their Lord.

But watchman, *when does the morning come*? The Bridegroom delays. Are there no signs of his coming out as the Sun of Righteousness? Hasn’t the morning star risen as the pledge of day? When will the day dawn and the shadows flee away? O Jesus, if you don’t come in person to your waiting church today, at least come in Spirit to my sighing heart and make it sing for joy.

modern:
This is a large request. To pray for a whole city takes a stretch of faith, and there are times when a prayer for one man is enough to stagger us. But how far-reaching the psalmist’s dying prayer was! How comprehensive! How sublime! “Let the whole earth be filled with his glory.” It doesn’t leave out a single country, however crushed under the foot of superstition; it doesn’t exclude a single nation, however barbarous. This prayer is offered for the cannibal as well as the civilized, for every climate and race; it takes in the whole circle of the earth and leaves out no son of Adam. We must be up and working for our Master, or we can’t honestly pray such a prayer. The request isn’t made with a sincere heart unless we try, as God helps us, to spread our Master’s kingdom. Aren’t there some who *neglect* both to pray and to work?

Reader, is it *your* prayer? Turn your eyes to Calvary. See the Lord of Life nailed to a cross, with the crown of thorns around his brow, with bleeding head and hands and feet. What! Can you look at this miracle of miracles, the death of the Son of God, without feeling in your heart a marvelous adoration that language can never express? And when you feel the blood applied to your conscience and know that he has blotted out your sins, *you are not a man* unless you jump up from your knees and cry, “Let the whole earth be filled with his glory; Amen, and Amen.” Can you bow before the Crucified in loving worship and not want to see your King master of the world? Shame on you, if you can pretend to love your Prince and not want to see him ruling over all. Your godliness is worthless unless it makes you want the same mercy that has reached you to bless the whole world. Lord, it is harvest time; put in your sickle and reap.

notes.term: Let the whole earth be filled with his glory
notes.note: The close of Psalm 72, followed by “The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended” ([[Ps.72.19-Ps.72.20|Psalm 72:19–20]]), which is why Spurgeon calls it a dying prayer.

modern:
Believers love Jesus with a deeper love than they dare give to anyone else. They would sooner lose father and mother than part with Christ. They hold all earthly comforts with a loose hand, but they carry him locked tight in their hearts. They willingly deny themselves for his sake, but they can’t be driven to *deny* him. It is a thin love that the fire of persecution can dry up; the true believer’s love is a deeper stream than that. People have worked hard to separate the faithful from their Master, but their attempts have failed in every age. Neither crowns of honor nor frowns of anger have untied this knot, tighter than the Gordian knot. This is no everyday attachment that the world’s power can dissolve in the end. Neither man nor devil has found a key that opens this lock. Satan’s cunning has never been more at a loss than when he has used it to try to tear apart this union of two hearts welded together by God. It is written, and nothing can blot out the sentence: “*The upright love thee*.”

The intensity of the love of the upright, however, isn’t to be judged so much by how it appears as by what the upright long for. It is our daily lament that we can’t love enough. We wish our hearts could hold more and reach further. Like Samuel Rutherford, we sigh and cry, “Oh, for as much love as would go round about the earth, and over heaven—yea, the heaven of heavens, and ten thousand worlds—that I might let all out upon fair, fair, only fair Christ.” Sadly, our longest reach is only a handspan of love, and our love is only a drop from a bucket compared with what he deserves. Measure our love by what we mean it to be, and it is high indeed; this is how, we trust, our Lord judges it. Oh, that we could give all the love in all hearts in one great mass, a gathering of all loves together, to him who is altogether lovely!

modern:
Ever since the first hour when goodness came into conflict with evil, it has always been true in spiritual experience that Satan hinders us. From every point of the compass, all along the line of battle, in the vanguard and in the rear, at dawn and at midnight, Satan hinders us. If we work in the field, he tries to break the plowshare; if we build the wall, he works to knock down the stones; if we try to serve God in suffering or in conflict, everywhere Satan hinders us. He hinders us when we first come to Jesus Christ. We had fierce conflicts with Satan when we first looked to the cross and lived. Now that we are saved, he tries to hinder our personal character from becoming complete. You may be congratulating yourself: “Up to now I have walked consistently; no one can challenge my integrity.” Beware of boasting, for your virtue will still be tested. Satan will aim his siege engines at the very virtue you are most famous for. If you have been a firm believer until now, your faith will soon be attacked; if you have been as meek as Moses, expect to be tempted to speak rashly with your lips. The birds will peck at your ripest fruit, and the wild boar will dash his tusks at your choicest vines.

Satan is sure to hinder us when we are earnest in prayer. He checks our persistence and weakens our faith, so that, if possible, we may miss the blessing. Nor is Satan any less watchful in blocking Christian effort. There was never a revival of religion without a revival of his opposition. As soon as Ezra and Nehemiah begin to work, Sanballat and Tobiah are stirred up to hinder them. What then? We aren’t alarmed because Satan hinders us, for it proves that we are on the Lord’s side and doing the Lord’s work; and in his strength we will win the victory and triumph over our enemy.

modern:
Look at the spider’s web, and see in it a most suggestive picture of the hypocrite’s religion. *It is meant to catch his prey*: the spider grows fat on flies, and the Pharisee has his reward. Foolish people are easily caught by the loud claims of pretenders, and even the more discerning can’t always escape. Philip baptized Simon Magus, whose deceitful declaration of faith was so soon blown apart by Peter’s stern rebuke. Custom, reputation, praise, advancement and other flies are the small game that hypocrites take in their nets. A spider’s web is *a marvel of skill*: look at it and admire the cunning hunter’s tricks. Isn’t a deceiver’s religion just as amazing? How does he make so barefaced a lie look like the truth? How can he make his tinsel pass so well for gold? A spider’s web *comes entirely out of the creature’s own body*. The bee gathers her wax from flowers; the spider sucks no flowers, and yet she spins out her material to any length. In the same way, hypocrites find their trust and hope within themselves. Their anchor was forged on their own anvil, and their cable twisted by their own hands. They lay their own foundation and cut the pillars of their own house, scorning to be in debt to the sovereign grace of God.

But a spider’s web is *very frail*. It is skillfully made, but not made to last. It is no match for the servant’s broom or the traveler’s staff. The hypocrite needs no battery of Armstrong guns to blow his hope to pieces; a mere puff of wind will do it. Hypocritical cobwebs will soon come down when the broom of destruction begins its cleansing work. Which brings us to one more thought, namely, that such cobwebs *are not to be put up with in the Lord’s house*. He will make sure that they, and those who spin them, are destroyed forever. O my soul, be resting on something better than a spider’s web. Let the Lord Jesus be your eternal hiding place.

notes.note: Isaiah on the schemes of the wicked: “their webs shall not become garments” ([[Isa.59.5-Isa.59.6|Isaiah 59:5–6]]). Compare the hypocrite “whose trust shall be a spider’s web” ([[Job.8.13-Job.8.14|Job 8:13–14]]).

modern:
Many who claim to be Christians are always doubting and fearing, and they gloomily think this is the necessary state of believers. That is a mistake, for “all things are possible to him that believeth”; and it is possible for us to climb to a state where a doubt or a fear will be only like a migrating bird, flitting across the soul but never lingering there. When you read of the high and sweet fellowship enjoyed by favored saints, you sigh and grumble in the privacy of your heart, “Ah, these aren’t for me.” Climber, if only you have faith, you will yet stand on the sunny pinnacle of the temple, for “all things are possible to him that believeth.” You hear of great deeds that holy men have done for Jesus: what they have enjoyed of him, how like him they have been, how they have been able to endure great persecutions for his sake; and you say, “Ah, as for me, I’m only a worm; I could never reach that.” But there is nothing any saint was that you can’t be. There is no height of grace, no level of spirituality, no clearness of assurance, no post of duty that isn’t open to you, if only you have the power to believe.

Lay aside your sackcloth and ashes, and rise to the dignity of your true position. You are little in Israel because you choose to be, not because there is any need for it. It isn’t fitting for you to grovel in the dust, child of a King. Climb up! The golden throne of assurance is waiting for you! The crown of fellowship with Jesus is ready to adorn your brow. Wrap yourself in scarlet and fine linen, and feast in splendor every day; for if you believe, you may eat the finest of the wheat. Your land will flow with milk and honey, and your soul will be satisfied as with marrow and fatness. Gather golden sheaves of grace, for they are waiting for you in the fields of faith. *“All things are possible to him that believeth.”*

modern: Up there in the better world, the inhabitants don’t depend on any created comforts. They need no clothes; their white robes never wear out, and they will never be stained. They need no medicine to heal diseases, “for the inhabitant shall not say, I am sick.” They need no sleep to restore their bodies; they don’t rest day or night, but tirelessly praise him in his temple. They need no human relationships to comfort them; whatever happiness they may get from the company of others isn’t essential to their joy, for their Lord’s company is enough for their largest desires. They need no teachers there. No doubt they talk with one another about the things of God, but they don’t need this for instruction; they will all be taught by the Lord. Ours are the handouts at the king’s gate, but they feast at the table itself. Here we lean on a friendly arm, but there they lean on their Beloved, and on him alone. Here we must have the help of our companions, but there they find everything they want in Christ Jesus. Here we look to the food that perishes and to the clothes that decay before the moth, but there they find everything in God. We use the bucket to draw water from the well, but there they drink from the source itself and put their lips down to the living water. Here the angels bring us blessings, but we will need no messengers from heaven then. They will need no Gabriels there to bring them love notes from God, for there they will see *him* face to face. Oh, what a blessed time that will be, when we have risen above every second cause and rest on the bare arm of God! What a glorious hour, when God and not his creatures, the Lord and not his works, will be our daily joy! Then our souls will have reached the perfection of happiness.

modern:
Mary of Magdala was *the victim of a terrible evil*. She was possessed not by one devil only, but by seven. These dreadful lodgers caused great pain and defilement to the poor body they had taken up residence in. Hers was a hopeless, horrible case. She couldn’t help herself, and no human help could do any good. But Jesus passed that way, and, unasked, and probably even resisted by the poor possessed woman, he spoke the word of power, and Mary of Magdala became *a trophy of the healing power of Jesus*. All seven demons left her, left her never to return, thrown out by force by the Lord of all. What a blessed deliverance! What a happy change! From madness to delight, from despair to peace, from hell to heaven!

At once she became *a constant follower of Jesus*, catching every word he said, following his wandering steps, sharing his hard-working life; and on top of that she became *his generous helper*, first among that band of healed and grateful women who supported him out of their own means. When Jesus was lifted up on the cross, Mary stayed *the sharer of his shame*. We find her first watching from far off, and then coming near to the foot of the cross. She couldn’t die on the cross with Jesus, but she stood as near it as she could; and when his blessed body was taken down, she watched to see how and where it was laid. She was *the faithful and watchful believer*, last at the tomb where Jesus slept, first at the grave he rose from. Her holy faithfulness made her *a favored witness of her beloved Rabboni*, who stooped to call her by name and to make her *his messenger of good news* to the trembling disciples and Peter. So grace found her a madwoman and made her a messenger; drove out devils and let her see angels; rescued her from Satan and joined her forever to the Lord Jesus. May I also be such a miracle of grace!

modern:
Paul’s marvelously rich phrase shows that Christ is the *source* of our life. “You hath he quickened who were dead in trespasses and sins.” The same voice that brought Lazarus out of the tomb raised us to newness of life. He is now the *substance* of our spiritual life. It is by his life that we live. He is in us, the hope of glory, the spring of our actions, the central thought that moves every other thought. *Christ is the food of our life*. What can the Christian feed on but Jesus’ flesh and blood? “This is the bread which cometh down from heaven, that a man may eat thereof, and not die.” Weary pilgrims in this wilderness of sin, you never get a bite to satisfy the hunger of your spirits unless you find it in him! *Christ is the comfort of our life*. All our true joys come from him, and in times of trouble his presence is our consolation. There is nothing worth living for but him, and his loving kindness is better than life!

*Christ is the aim of our life*. As the ship speeds toward port, so the believer hurries toward the harbor of his Savior’s breast. As the arrow flies to its target, so the Christian flies toward the perfecting of his fellowship with Christ Jesus. As the soldier fights for his captain and is crowned in his captain’s victory, so the believer fights for Christ and gets his triumph out of the triumphs of his Master. “For him to live is Christ.” *Christ is the model of our life*. Where the same life is within, there will be, there must be, to a great extent, the same results without; and if we live in close fellowship with the Lord Jesus, we will grow like him. We will set him before us as our divine pattern and try to walk in his footsteps, until he becomes *the crown of our life in glory*. Oh, how safe, how honored, how happy the Christian is, since Christ is our life!

notes.note: “When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory” ([[Col.3.4|Colossians 3:4]]).

modern:
See one of the great Physician’s mightiest skills: he has power to forgive sin! While he lived here below, before the ransom had been paid, before the blood had literally been sprinkled on the mercy-seat, he had power to forgive sin. Hasn’t he power to do it now that he has died? What power must live in him who has faithfully paid his people’s debts to the last penny! He has boundless power now that he has finished transgression and made an end of sin. If you doubt it, see him rising from the dead! See him ascending in splendor to the right hand of God! Hear him pleading before the eternal Father, pointing to his wounds, pressing the merit of his sacred sufferings! What power to forgive is here! “He hath ascended on high, and received gifts for men.” “He is exalted on high to give repentance and remission of sins.” The most crimson sins are removed by the crimson of his blood.

At this moment, dear reader, whatever your sinfulness, Christ has power to pardon; power to pardon *you*, and millions like you. A word will do it. He has nothing more to do to win your pardon; all the atoning work is done. In answer to your tears, he can forgive your sins today and make you know it. At this very moment he can breathe into your soul a peace with God that passes all understanding, springing from the complete forgiveness of your many sins. Do you believe that? I trust you do. May you experience now the power of Jesus to forgive sin! Waste no time in going to the Physician of souls, but hurry to him with words like these:

modern:
Great numbers of Christians look on the past with pleasure but on the present with dissatisfaction. They look back on the days they spent in fellowship with the Lord as the sweetest and best they have ever known, but the present is dressed in the black clothes of gloom and dreariness. Once they lived close to Jesus, but now they feel they have wandered from him, and they say, “O that I were as in months past!” They complain that they have lost their evidences, or that they have no present peace of mind, or no enjoyment in the means of grace, or that their conscience isn’t as tender, or that they don’t have as much zeal for God’s glory.

The causes of this sad state of things are many. It may come from a relative *neglect of prayer*, for a neglected prayer closet is the beginning of all spiritual decline. Or it may be the result of *idolatry*. The heart has been taken up with something else more than with God; the affections have been set on the things of earth instead of the things of heaven. A jealous God won’t be content with a divided heart; he must be loved first and best. He will withdraw the sunshine of his presence from a cold, wandering heart. Or the cause may be found in *self-confidence* and *self-righteousness*. Pride is busy in the heart, and self is lifted up instead of lying low at the foot of the cross.

Christian, if you aren’t now as you “were in months past,” don’t rest content with *wishing* for your old happiness back. Go at once and look for your Master, and tell him your sad state. Ask his grace and strength to help you walk more closely with him. Humble yourself before him, and he will lift you up and let you enjoy the light of his face once again. Don’t sit down to sigh and grieve. While the beloved Physician lives there is hope; no, there is certainty of recovery for the worst cases.

modern:
“Consolation.” There is music in the word; like David’s harp, it charms away the evil spirit of melancholy. It was a great honor for Barnabas to be called “the son of consolation”; yes, it is one of the glorious names of one greater than Barnabas, for the Lord Jesus is “the consolation of Israel.” “*Everlasting* consolation”: here is the cream of it all, for the eternity of the comfort is its crown and glory. What is this “everlasting consolation”? It includes a sense of pardoned sin. A Christian has received in his heart the witness of the Spirit that his sins are put away like a cloud, and his wrongdoings like a thick cloud. If sin is pardoned, isn’t that an everlasting consolation?

Next, the Lord gives his people a lasting sense of being accepted in Christ. The Christian knows that God sees him as standing in union with Jesus. Union with the risen Lord is a comfort of the most lasting kind; in fact, it is everlasting. Let sickness lay us low: haven’t we seen hundreds of believers as happy in the weakness of disease as they would have been in strong, glowing health? Let death’s arrows pierce us to the heart: our comfort doesn’t die, for haven’t our ears very often heard the songs of saints rejoicing because the living love of God was poured out in their hearts in their dying moments? Yes, a sense of being accepted in the Beloved is an everlasting consolation. Moreover, the Christian has a conviction that he is secure. God has promised to save those who trust in Christ; the Christian does trust in Christ, and he believes that God will be as good as his word and will save him. He feels that he is safe because he is bound up with the person and work of Jesus.

notes.note: “God, even our Father, which hath loved us, and hath given us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace” ([[2Thess.2.16|2 Thessalonians 2:16]]). Consolation means comfort.

modern: There is no cause at all for unease as long as this blessed sentence is true. *On earth*, the Lord’s power controls the rage of the wicked as easily as the rage of the sea; his love refreshes the poor with mercy as easily as the earth with showers. Majesty gleams in flashes of fire amid the horrors of the storm, and the glory of the Lord is seen in its grandeur in the fall of empires and the crash of thrones. In all our conflicts and troubles we may see the hand of the divine King.

*In hell*, evil spirits acknowledge his undoubted supremacy, to their misery. When they are allowed to roam about, it is with a chain at their heels; the bit is in the mouth of behemoth, and the hook in the jaws of leviathan. Death’s arrows are under the Lord’s lock, and the grave’s prisons have divine power as their jailer. The terrible vengeance of the Judge of all the earth makes devils cower and tremble, like dogs in the kennel afraid of the huntsman’s whip.

*In heaven*, no one doubts the sovereignty of the eternal King; all fall on their faces to worship him. Angels are his courtiers, the redeemed his favorites, and all delight to serve him day and night. May we soon reach the city of the great King!

notes.term: The Lord reigneth, let the earth rejoice

modern:
The rainbow, the sign of the covenant with Noah, is a picture of our Lord Jesus, who is the Lord’s witness to the people. When can we *expect to see the sign of the covenant*? The rainbow can only be seen painted on a *cloud*. When the sinner’s conscience is dark with clouds, when he remembers his past sin and mourns and grieves before God, Jesus Christ is revealed to him as the covenant Rainbow, showing all the glorious colors of God’s character and promising peace. For the believer, when trials and temptations surround him, it is sweet to see the person of our Lord Jesus Christ: to see him bleeding, living, rising and pleading for us. God’s rainbow is hung over the cloud of our sins, our sorrows and our troubles, to foretell deliverance.

Nor does a *cloud* alone make a rainbow; there must be *the crystal drops* to reflect the light of the sun. So our sorrows mustn’t only threaten; they must really fall on us. There would have been no Christ for us if the vengeance of God had been only a threatening cloud: punishment had to fall in terrible drops on the Surety. Until there is *real* anguish in the sinner’s conscience, there is no Christ for him; until the discipline he feels becomes painful, he can’t see Jesus. But there must also be a sun, for clouds and drops of rain don’t make rainbows unless the sun shines. Dear friends, our God, who is like the sun to us, always shines, but we don’t always see him; clouds hide his face. But whatever drops may be falling, or whatever clouds may be threatening, if only *he* shines, there will be a rainbow at once. It is said that when we see the rainbow, the shower is over. Certainly, when Christ comes, our troubles go; when we see Jesus, our sins vanish, and our doubts and fears die down. When Jesus walks on the waters of the sea, how deep the calm!

modern:
Lebanon’s cedars are a picture of the Christian, in that *they owe their planting entirely to the Lord*. This is quite true of every child of God. He isn’t planted by man or by himself, but by God. The mysterious hand of the divine Spirit dropped the living seed into a heart he had prepared himself to receive it. Every true heir of heaven acknowledges the great Gardener as the one who planted him. Moreover, the cedars of Lebanon *don’t depend on man for their watering*. They stand on the high rock, untouched by human irrigation, and yet our heavenly Father supplies them. So it is with the Christian who has learned to live by faith. He is independent of man, even in earthly things; for his continued support he looks to the Lord his God, and to him alone. The dew of heaven is his portion, and the God of heaven is his fountain.

Again, the cedars of Lebanon *aren’t protected by any human power*. They owe nothing to man for their protection from stormy wind and tempest. They are God’s trees, kept and preserved by him, and by him alone. It is exactly the same with the Christian. He isn’t a hothouse plant, sheltered from temptation; he stands in the most exposed position. He has no shelter, no protection, except this: that the broad wings of the eternal God always cover the cedars he himself has planted. Like cedars, believers are *full of sap*, with life enough to stay green even in the winter snows. Lastly, the flourishing and majestic state of the cedar *is to the praise of God alone*. The Lord, the Lord alone, has been everything to the cedars, and so David puts it very sweetly in one of the psalms: “Praise ye the Lord, fruitful trees and all cedars.” In the believer there is nothing that can make much of man. He is planted, fed and protected by the Lord’s own hand, and to him let all the glory be given.

modern:
Notice the shape of the promise. God doesn’t say, “And when ye shall look upon the bow, and *ye* shall remember my covenant, *then* I will not destroy the earth.” It is gloriously put not on *our* memory, which is fickle and frail, but on *God’s* memory, which is infinite and unchanging. “The bow shall be in the cloud; and I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant.” Oh, it isn’t my remembering God but God’s remembering *me* that is the ground of my safety; it isn’t my taking hold of his covenant but his covenant’s taking hold of me. Glory be to God! All the walls of salvation are made secure by divine power, and even the lesser towers, which we might imagine could have been left to man, are guarded by almighty strength. Even the *remembering* of the covenant isn’t left to our memories, for *we* might forget; but our Lord can’t forget the saints he has engraved on the palms of his hands.

It is with us as it was with Israel in Egypt. The blood was on the lintel and the two side posts, but the Lord didn’t say, “When *you* see the blood I will pass over you,” but “When *I* see the blood I will pass over you.” My looking to Jesus brings me joy and peace, but it is God’s looking to Jesus that secures my salvation and that of all his chosen, since it is impossible for our God to look at Christ, our bleeding Surety, and then be angry with us for sins already punished in him. No, it isn’t left to *us* even to be saved by remembering the covenant. There is no mixed cloth here; not a single thread of the creature spoils the fabric. It isn’t *of* man, nor *by* man, but of the Lord alone. We *should* remember the covenant, and by God’s grace we *will*; but the hinge of our safety doesn’t hang there. It is God’s remembering *us*, not our remembering *him*; and so the covenant is *an everlasting covenant*.

modern:
Do you believe that your sins are forgiven, and that Christ has made full atonement for them? Then what a joyful Christian *you ought to be*! How you should live above the ordinary trials and troubles of the world! Since your sin is forgiven, can it matter what happens to you now? Luther said, “Smite, Lord, smite, for my sin is forgiven; if thou hast but forgiven me, smite as hard as thou wilt”; and in the same spirit you can say, “Send sickness, poverty, losses, crosses, persecution, whatever you will; *you have forgiven me*, and my soul is glad.”

Christian, if you are saved like this, then while you are glad, *be grateful and loving*. Cling to the cross that took your sin away; serve the one who served you. “I beseech you therefore, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” Don’t let your zeal evaporate in some little bubbling-over of song. Show your love in practical ways. Love the brothers and sisters of the one who loved you. If there is a Mephibosheth anywhere who is lame or crippled, help him for Jonathan’s sake. If there is a poor, tried believer, weep with him, and carry his cross for the sake of the one who wept for you and carried your sins. Since you are forgiven so freely for Christ’s sake, go and tell others the joyful news of pardoning mercy. Don’t be content to keep this indescribable blessing for yourself alone, but spread abroad the story of the cross. Holy gladness and holy boldness will make you a good preacher, and the whole world will be a pulpit for you to preach in. Cheerful holiness is the most powerful of sermons, but the Lord must give it to you. Seek it this morning before you go out into the world. When it is the Lord’s work we are rejoicing in, we needn’t be afraid of being too glad.

modern: The child is cheered as he sings, “This my father knows”; and shouldn’t we be comforted when we see that our dear Friend, the tender husband of our souls, knows all about us?

1. *He is the Physician*, and if he knows everything, the patient doesn’t need to. Hush, you silly, fluttering heart, prying, peeping and suspecting! What you don’t know now, you will know later; and meanwhile Jesus, the beloved Physician, knows your soul in its troubles. Why should the patient analyze all the medicine or weigh up all the symptoms? That is the Physician’s work, not mine. It is my business to trust, and his to prescribe. If he writes his prescription in strange handwriting I can’t read, I won’t be uneasy about it, but will rely on his unfailing skill to make it all plain in the result, however mysterious it is in the working.

2. *He is the Master*, and his knowledge is to serve us instead of our own. We are to obey, not to judge: “The servant knoweth not what his lord doeth.” Should the architect explain his plans to every laborer carrying bricks on the site? If he knows what he intends, isn’t that enough? The pot on the wheel can’t guess what pattern it will be shaped to, but if the potter understands his craft, what does the clay’s ignorance matter? My Lord mustn’t be cross-examined any more by someone as ignorant as I am.

3. *He is the Head*. All understanding is centered there. What judgment does the arm have? What understanding does the foot have? All the power to know lies in the head. Why should a limb have a brain of its own, when the head does all its thinking for it? Here, then, the believer must rest his comfort in sickness: not that he himself can see the end, but that Jesus knows everything. Sweet Lord, be forever eye and soul and head for us, and let us be content to know only what you choose to reveal.
